pos: n. (weakness, especially of the hands; the collapse of a man's grip under terror)
etymology: From Old French feble, from Latin flebilis, lamentable, from flere, to weep. At Jeremiah 47:3 it renders Hebrew riphyon, a slackening or sinking, from raphah, to let drop.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah is describing the Philistine coast under the approach of an army, and the horror is located in one detail: At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his strong horses, at the rushing of his chariots, and at the rumbling of his wheels, the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands. The prophet does not describe the killing. He describes fathers running and not turning round. The Hebrew word is a slackening, a letting-drop, and it is used of hands because the hands are where terror shows first — a man whose hands have gone will not carry a child.

The Bible uses this bodily fact as a standing figure for the loss of courage. Ezekiel: All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water. Nahum, over Nineveh: the heart melteth, and the knees smite together. And because it is a figure, it can be reversed by a word. Isaiah gives the command that the writer to the Hebrews later takes up almost verbatim: Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees, which Hebrews turns into lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees and sets in the middle of a passage on chastening. That is the New Testament's pastoral use of the word. Hands that hang down are not rebuked; they are lifted, and the argument used to lift them is that the Father who is disciplining them is dealing with them as with sons.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): weakness; imbecility; want of strength; infirmity of body.
webster_full: FEEBLENESS, n. Weakness of body or of mind; imbecility; infirmity; want of strength.
FEEBLE, a. Weak; destitute of much physical strength; infirm; debilitated.
SLACKEN, v.i. To become less tense, firm or rigid; to lose strength or intensity.
CONFIRM, v.t. To make firm or more firm; to add strength to; to strengthen.
RUMBLING, ppr. Making a low, heavy, continued sound, as of thunder or of wheels.
scriptures: Jeremiah 47:3

At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his strong horses, at the rushing of his chariots, and at the rumbling of his wheels, the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands;
Ezekiel 7:17
All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water.
Isaiah 35:3
Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees.
Hebrews 12:12
Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees;
corruption_summary: Discouragement is treated either as a moral failure to be scolded or as a condition to be managed, where Scripture commands the strong to go and strengthen the hands that have dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Two responses to a discouraged Christian both miss what Isaiah and Hebrews prescribe. The first tells him to pull himself together, which is precisely what feeble hands cannot do; the second files him permanently under the weak and stops expecting anything of him. The biblical command is in the imperative and is addressed to somebody else: Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees. Hebrews places that command in the middle of a chapter about the Father's discipline, which means the strengthening is done with truth — you are a son, this is a Father's hand, the end of it is the peaceable fruit of righteousness — and not with sentiment.

The second thing to hold is the picture's honesty. Jeremiah 47 is a father who does not look back at his own child because his hands have failed him. Scripture does not pretend that faith exempts a man from the body's reactions to terror. Isaiah 40 says the youths shall faint and be weary and the young men shall utterly fall, and then, in the same breath, that they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength. The strength is renewed; it is not native. That is why the cure in every one of these passages comes from outside the man — a word spoken to him, a hand lifting his.
roots_summary: Hebrew riphyon (H7510), a slackening; raphah (H7503), to let drop, to be slack; Greek paraluo (G3886), to weaken or paralyse.
roots_lines: Hebrew riphyon (H7510) — a slackness, a sinking; used once, of the hands of fleeing fathers.
Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to sink, to let drop; the same root as be still in Be still, and know that I am God.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, to make firm; Isaiah's command over the weak hands.
Greek paraluo (G3886) — to loose alongside, to enfeeble; the participle in Hebrews 12:12.
Greek anorthoo (G461) — to set upright again; lift up the hands which hang down.
usage: “the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands” — terror located in the grip.
“Strengthen ye the weak hands” — a command addressed to somebody else.
“lift up the hands which hang down” — set in a chapter about a Father's discipline.

pos: n. (a failing of heart; in Leviticus 26, a judgment sent into the hearts of the scattered)
etymology: From Old French feint, feigned or sluggish, from Latin fingere. At Leviticus 26:36 it renders Hebrew morek, softness or timidity — the AV's only use of the noun.
biblical_def:
Among the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 is one that touches nothing outside a man: And upon them that are left alive of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth. The Hebrew word is softness. It is not sent against their cities or their harvests; it is sent into their hearts, and the effect described is the most humiliating in the chapter — grown men running from a leaf.

Scripture treats courage as a gift and cowardice as a judgment, and the pairing is exact. The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion. Both halves are supernatural. The wicked man's panic is not merely nerves; it is the sentence of Leviticus 26 falling on a conscience that knows what it has done. And the righteous man's boldness is not temperament; it is the fruit of being at peace with God. Isaiah puts the positive side in the plainest promise in the prophets, and every clause of it is a remedy for the softness of Leviticus: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): want of strength or vigor; feebleness; timorousness; dejection of mind.
webster_full: FAINTNESS, n. Want of strength or vigor; feebleness; also, timorousness; dejection; loss of courage.
FAINT, a. Weak; languid; inclined to swoon; also, cowardly; timorous; dejected.
TIMOROUS, a. Fearful of danger; timid; destitute of courage; fearful.
DISMAY, v.t. To deprive of that strength or firmness of mind which constitutes courage; to discourage.
PURSUE, v.t. To follow; to go or proceed after or in a like direction; to chase.
scriptures: Leviticus 26:36

And upon them that are left alive of you I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies; and the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them; and they shall flee, as fleeing from a sword; and they shall fall when none pursueth.
Leviticus 26:37
And they shall fall one upon another, as it were before a sword, when none pursueth: and ye shall have no power to stand before your enemies.
Proverbs 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
Isaiah 41:10
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
corruption_summary: Anxiety is handled exclusively as a medical or psychological category, and the biblical possibility that a fearful heart may be a judgment, or that boldness may be a gift, is never raised.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 26 says God sent a faintness into the hearts of a covenant-breaking people, and Proverbs says the wicked flee when no man pursueth. These are moral and spiritual statements about fear, and a Christian account of the fearful heart has to make room for them. That does not mean every anxious believer is under judgment; it plainly means some fear is. Where a man's heart accuses him, the first help he needs is not a technique but the blood of Christ, and 1 John states the order exactly: if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things.

The opposite error must be refused just as firmly. Scripture knows fear that is not judgment at all: Elijah under the juniper tree was given sleep and food before he was given a word; Paul says he was troubled on every side, without were fightings, within were fears; and the Lord Jesus in the garden was sorrowful unto death. A pastor who treats every anxious member as a covenant-breaker has misread Leviticus 26 as badly as the counsellor who has never read it. The remedy offered in Scripture is neither diagnosis nor scolding but a Person speaking: Fear thou not; for I am with thee.
roots_summary: Hebrew morek (H4816), softness, timidity; raph (H7390), tender or faint; Greek ekluo (G1590), to faint or grow weary.
roots_lines: Hebrew morek (H4816) — softness, faintness; used once, sent into the heart as a judgment.
Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue, to chase; what the sound of a leaf was said to do.
Hebrew nus (H5127) — to flee; the wicked fleeing when none pursueth.
Greek ekluo (G1590) — to loosen out, and so to faint; let us not be weary in well doing.
Greek deilia (G1167) — timidity, cowardice; God hath not given us the spirit of fear.
usage: “I will send a faintness into their hearts” — a judgment aimed inside a man.
“the sound of a shaken leaf shall chase them” — the most humiliating curse in the chapter.
“the righteous are bold as a lion” — courage as a fruit, not a temperament.

pos: adj. (in poor health; at Corinth, the physical consequence of unworthy communion)
etymology: From Old English seoc, ill. At 1 Corinthians 11:30 it renders Greek arrhostos, without strength, infirm — the same word used of the few sick folk our Lord healed at Nazareth.
biblical_def:
Paul has been rebuking the Corinthians for the way they came to the Lord's table — one hungry, another drunken, the poor shamed — and he states a consequence that the modern church finds very hard to hear: For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep. Weak, sickly, and dead. He is not speaking figuratively; many sleep is his usual term for believers who have died, and he is naming real illness and real graves in a real congregation as the Lord's discipline for how they handled the Supper.

The passage is guarded on both sides so that it cannot be turned into cruelty. Paul does not tell the sick to stay away; he tells everyone to examine himself and so let him eat. He says the chastening is precisely so that they should not be condemned with the world — it is a Father's rod, not a judge's sentence. And he gives the way out in a single verse: if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. The New Testament also rules out the reverse error of reading every illness as a verdict. Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick; Timothy had his often infirmities; Epaphroditus was sick nigh unto death in the Lord's own work; and the man born blind was blind that the works of God should be made manifest in him. James's instruction to the sick assumes no guilt at all — call for the elders, and let them pray.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): not healthy; somewhat disordered in health; habitually indisposed.
webster_full: SICKLY, a. Not healthy; somewhat affected with disease; habitually indisposed; infirm.
SICKNESS, n. Disease; malady; a morbid state of the body of an animal, in which the organs do not perform their functions.
INFIRM, a. Not firm or sound; weak; feeble; as an infirm body.
EXAMINE, v.t. To inspect carefully, with a view to discover truth or the real state of things.
CHASTEN, v.t. To correct by punishment; to punish; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 11:30
For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep.
1 Corinthians 11:28
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
1 Corinthians 11:31
For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.
James 5:14
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
corruption_summary: Illness is read either as always a sign of hidden sin or as never having anything to do with it; Scripture refuses both and puts the burden on self-examination rather than on diagnosis of others.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching makes sickness a symptom of insufficient faith and so adds the cruelty of accusation to the weight of disease. It cannot survive the New Testament's own examples: Paul's thorn, which God refused to remove and explained; Trophimus left sick; Timothy's stomach; Epaphroditus near death in gospel work; and the Lord's own verdict on the man born blind, that neither he nor his parents had sinned. A theology that cannot account for a sick apostle's companion is not reading the same book.

The opposite drift, more common in respectable churches, is to treat 1 Corinthians 11:30 as though Paul had not written it — to conclude that God never disciplines bodily and that the Supper carries no danger. Paul says otherwise, plainly, about a church he loved. The pastoral resolution is the one he supplies: no one is authorized to diagnose anyone else, and everyone is commanded to examine himself. Job's comforters are the standing warning against the first; Corinth is the warning against the second.
roots_summary: Greek arrhostos (G732), without strength, sickly; asthenes (G772), weak; koimao (G2837), to fall asleep, to die.
roots_lines: Greek arrhostos (G732) — infirm, sickly; literally not strong.
Greek asthenes (G772) — without strength, weak; the first word in Paul's triple.
Greek koimao (G2837) — to fall asleep; the New Testament's word for the death of a believer.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; let a man examine himself.
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to train a child, to chasten; the Lord's dealing at Corinth, not condemnation.
usage: “many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep” — a consequence named plainly.
“let a man examine himself, and so let him eat” — examine, and come.
“Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders” — no guilt assumed.

pos: v. (fainted from hunger; of the children in the streets of Jerusalem during the siege)
etymology: From Old English geswogen, overcome. At Lamentations 2:12 it renders Hebrew ataph, to cover over, to grow faint — used of a soul enveloped and failing.
biblical_def:
Lamentations 2 is Jeremiah walking through the ruin of the city he had spent forty years warning, and the verse is unbearable: They say to their mothers, Where is corn and wine? when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers' bosom. Children asking for bread, fainting like men with sword wounds, and dying in their mothers' arms. The prophet who had been called a traitor for foretelling this is the one who writes it down, and he does not write it coldly: Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth.

What he does with the grief is the reason the book is in the canon. He does not resolve it, explain it away, or hurry to the third chapter's mercies as though the second had not happened. He tells the city to pray: Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street. That is what Scripture does with a horror it has itself announced as just judgment — it sends the sufferer to the same God, at night, with his hands up. And it is only after two chapters of this that the great lines arrive: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): fainted; fell into a fainting fit; lost consciousness through weakness.
webster_full: SWOON, v.i. To faint; to sink into a fainting fit, in which there is a suspension of the apparent vital functions.
SWOONED, pp. Fainted; overcome; having fallen into a swoon.
FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.
LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.
BOSOM, n. The breast of a human being, and the parts adjacent; the folds or covering of clothes about the breast.
scriptures: Lamentations 2:12
They say to their mothers, Where is corn and wine? when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers' bosom.
Lamentations 2:11

Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city.
Lamentations 2:19

Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street.
Isaiah 51:20
Thy sons have fainted, they lie at the head of all the streets, as a wild bull in a net: they are full of the fury of the LORD, the rebuke of thy God.
corruption_summary: Lament has nearly disappeared from evangelical worship, and a church with no vocabulary for Lamentations 2 will have nothing to give its people when the streets fill.
corruption_paragraphs: Roughly a third of the Psalter is lament, an entire book of the canon is nothing else, and a great many congregations sing none of it. The result is predictable: believers meet real catastrophe with no words that the church has taught them, conclude that grief of this kind has no place among the faithful, and go through it privately while singing something cheerful on Sunday. The regulative principle cuts here in an unexpected direction. God has given His people words for this, in Scripture, and a worship that uses only the glad ones is not more biblical than one that uses both.

Lamentations also refuses the two evasions. It does not deny that the judgment was deserved — the book says repeatedly that the LORD has done what He purposed, that Jerusalem hath grievously sinned. And it does not let that verdict silence the grief; the same writer says his liver is poured upon the earth for the destruction of the daughter of his people. Both are true at once, and the book holds them for three chapters before it says his compassions fail not. That is the pattern for any Christian mourning a thing he knows was just.
roots_summary: Hebrew ataph (H5848), to be enveloped, to faint; shaphak (H8210), to pour out; qinah (H7015), a dirge.
roots_lines: Hebrew ataph (H5848) — to cover, to be overwhelmed and faint; the children swooning in the street.
Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out; used of the child's soul and of the heart poured out like water in prayer.
Hebrew qinah (H7015) — a lamentation, a funeral dirge; the acrostic form of the whole book.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant mercy; the plural in it is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed.
Hebrew emunah (H530) — faithfulness; great is thy faithfulness, three chapters after this verse.
usage: “when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city” — children dying like men under the sword.
“pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord” — what to do with it.
“Mine eyes do fail with tears” — the prophet who foretold it, weeping over it.

pos: n. (the colour drained from a face; in Jeremiah 30, the look of men in the time of Jacob's trouble)
etymology: From Old French pale, from Latin pallidus. At Jeremiah 30:6 it renders Hebrew yeraqon, a greenish or sallow colour — elsewhere the word for mildew on grain.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah is shown a day of trouble and describes it by what it does to men's bodies: Ask ye now, and see whether a man doth travail with child? wherefore do I see every man with his hands on his loins, as a woman in travail, and all faces are turned into paleness? The image is deliberately impossible. Men do not travail; yet the prophet sees every man standing in the posture of a woman in labour, hands on his loins, face gone sallow. The Hebrew word is the one used for the yellow blight on standing corn — the colour of something living turning the shade of something dying.

The next verse gives the day its name and its hope in one breath: Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it: it is even the time of Jacob's trouble; but he shall be saved out of it. That final clause is the reason the passage is not despair. The prophets use this bodily vocabulary consistently — Joel: all faces shall gather blackness; Nahum over Nineveh: the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness. Terror looks the same on every face in every century. What differs is whether there is a clause on the end of the sentence, and for Jacob there is: but he shall be saved out of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): want of color in the face; wanness; the appearance of a face deprived of its natural hue.
webster_full: PALENESS, n. Want of color or luster; wanness; defect of color in the human face.
PALE, a. White or somewhat white; wan; deficient in color; not ruddy or fresh of color.
TRAVAIL, n. Labor with pain; severe toil; also, the labor of childbirth.
LOINS, n. The space on each side of the vertebrae, between the lowest of the false ribs and the upper portion of the hip bone.
WAN, a. Pale; having a sickly hue; languid of look.
scriptures: Jeremiah 30:6
Ask ye now, and see whether a man doth travail with child? wherefore do I see every man with his hands on his loins, as a woman in travail, and all faces are turned into paleness?
Jeremiah 30:7
Alas! for that day is great, so that none is like it: it is even the time of Jacob's trouble; but he shall be saved out of it.
Joel 2:6
Before their face the people shall be much pained: all faces shall gather blackness.
Nahum 2:10
She is empty, and void, and waste: and the heart melteth, and the knees smite together, and much pain is in all loins, and the faces of them all gather blackness.
corruption_summary: The time of Jacob's trouble has been made the property of one prophetic system, and the promise attached to it — but he shall be saved out of it — gets lost in the charting.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 30:7 has become a fixture of dispensational prophecy charts, where it is assigned to a seven-year tribulation on a timetable Scripture nowhere lays out and which no Reformation confession contains. Whatever one's millennial position — and the Reformed tradition holds several — the phrase has a plain sense in its own chapter: a day of unequalled distress for the covenant people, out of which they are saved. Verses 8 to 11 continue in the same voice: I will break his yoke from off thy neck; I am with thee, saith the LORD, to save thee. The context is deliverance, not a schedule.

The other thing worth recovering is what the prophets do with terror. They report it accurately — hands on the loins, faces gone the colour of mildew — and they never leave it as the last word to a people in covenant. Every one of these passages that concerns Israel has a but in it. That is the shape of Christian hope under real fear: the fear is not denied, the body is not lied about, and the sentence does not end there.
roots_summary: Hebrew yeraqon (H3420), paleness, mildew; chalchalah (H2479), anguish, writhing; tsarah (H6869), trouble, distress.
roots_lines: Hebrew yeraqon (H3420) — a sallow greenish colour; elsewhere the mildew on standing grain.
Hebrew chalchalah (H2479) — writhing, anguish; the pain in the loins of Nahum 2:10.
Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — distress, trouble; the time of Jacob's trouble.
Hebrew chalats (H2504) — the loins; where the hands are placed in the prophets' picture of terror.
Hebrew yasha (H3467) — to save; the promise on the end of the sentence.
usage: “all faces are turned into paleness” — the colour of mildew on a living face.
“every man with his hands on his loins, as a woman in travail” — a deliberately impossible picture.
“but he shall be saved out of it” — the clause that changes the verse.

pos: n. (the state of being past life or fruitfulness; of Sarah's womb, which Abraham considered and believed anyway)
etymology: From Old English dead. At Romans 4:19 it renders Greek nekrosis, a putting to death or state of death — a strong clinical word, used of Sarah's barrenness at ninety.
biblical_def:
Paul is establishing that Abraham was justified by faith and not by works, and he refuses to make the patriarch's faith easy: And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb. The Greek word is nekrosis — the state of a corpse. Paul applies it to the reproductive prospects of a hundred-year-old man and a ninety-year-old woman and does not soften it, because the whole argument depends on there being nothing whatever in the circumstances to encourage belief.

The verse says he considered not, which does not mean he failed to notice. Genesis records that Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said in his heart, Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? He had done the arithmetic. What Paul means is that having weighed the deadness, he did not let it be the deciding weight: He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. Faith in Scripture is never the refusal to look at the facts. It is the conviction that the God who has spoken outranks them. And the same chapter identifies the God in question as the one who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were — which makes a dead womb precisely the sort of material He is known to work with.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): want of natural life or vital power; want of vigor; the state of being dead.
webster_full: DEADNESS, n. Want of natural life or vital power; want of animation; want of warmth or ardor.
BARREN, a. Not producing young; not prolific; unfruitful.
QUICKEN, v.t. To make alive; to vivify; to revive or resuscitate, as from death.
PERSUADE, v.t. To influence by argument or expostulation; to convince by proof; to bring to a settled belief.
STAGGER, v.i. To reel; to waver; to begin to doubt; to hesitate; to become less confident.
scriptures: Romans 4:19
And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb:
Romans 4:20
He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God;
Romans 4:21
And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.
Genesis 17:17
Then Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?
corruption_summary: Faith is redefined as a positive attitude that refuses to acknowledge difficulty, when Abraham's faith is described in the very verse that itemizes the impossibility.
corruption_paragraphs: A widespread teaching holds that to name a hard fact is to make room for unbelief — that a Christian should not speak of the diagnosis, the debt, or the barrenness, lest he undo the promise. Romans 4:19 destroys the idea in a sentence, because it is the Holy Ghost who lists the deadness. Paul names the age, the body, the womb, all three, and calls the man not weak in faith in the same breath. Faith that has not looked at anything is not faith; it is inattention. What Abraham did not do was let the facts overrule the word of the God who had spoken to him.

The verse also guards the character of saving faith itself. Paul's point in Romans 4 is not that Abraham had an impressive quality which earned him a son, but that he believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness — the righteousness reckoned, not achieved. This is the pivot of the Reformation doctrine of justification, and it hangs on the deadness: a man past fathering and a woman past bearing, so that when Isaac came there could be no question whose work he was. The same logic governs the sinner's salvation, and the same chapter names the God who does it — He quickeneth the dead.
roots_summary: Greek nekrosis (G3500), a state of death; nekroo (G3499), to put to death; zoopoieo (G2227), to quicken or make alive.
roots_lines: Greek nekrosis (G3500) — a putting to death, a dead state; used of Sarah's womb and of bearing about the dying of the Lord Jesus.
Greek nekroo (G3499) — to make dead; the perfect participle of Abraham's own body.
Greek zoopoieo (G2227) — to make alive; God quickeneth the dead in Romans 4:17.
Greek diakrino (G1252) — to waver, to be divided; he staggered not.
Greek plerophoreo (G4135) — to be fully carried, fully persuaded; Abraham's settled conviction.
usage: “neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb” — the Holy Ghost itemizing the impossibility.
“He staggered not at the promise of God” — the facts weighed, and outranked.
“what he had promised, he was able also to perform” — the ground of the whole.

pos: adv. (fatally; of a blow struck in hatred, which put the killer outside the protection of the cities of refuge)
etymology: From Latin mortalis, subject to death, from mors, death. At Deuteronomy 19:11 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning smite him in soul — to strike at the life.
biblical_def:
The law of the cities of refuge distinguishes two killers, and the distinction turns on the heart: But if any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him mortally that he die, and fleeth into one of these cities. Three elements make the difference — hatred beforehand, lying in wait, and a blow struck at the life. Such a man may run to the altar itself and shall be taken from it; the elders of his city are to fetch him out of the refuge and deliver him to the avenger of blood. The refuge was never a sanctuary for murder. It was protection for the man who killeth any person at unawares, and the law is careful to say so.

This is one of the places where Scripture is plainly more exact than the cultures around it and than a great deal of modern comment about it. The Mosaic code separates premeditated murder from manslaughter, provides an asylum and a trial, requires witnesses, and forbids a single witness to convict in a capital case. The manslayer stayed in the city until the death of the high priest, and then went free — a type no reader of Hebrews can miss, since the death of the true High Priest is what releases the guilty. And the same law forecloses any use of religion to shield a murderer: thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): in a deadly manner; so as to cause death; irrecoverably.
webster_full: MORTALLY, adv. Irrecoverably; in a manner that must cause death.
MORTAL, a. Subject to death; destined to die; deadly; destructive to life.
MANSLAYER, n. One who has killed a human being.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
AVENGER, n. One who avenges or vindicates; a vindicator; a revenger.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 19:11
But if any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him mortally that he die, and fleeth into one of these cities:
Numbers 35:11
Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
Exodus 21:14
But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die.
Proverbs 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
corruption_summary: The Mosaic judicials are dismissed as primitive, when the cities of refuge are among the earliest codifications anywhere of intent, asylum, trial and the rules of evidence.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern account treats Israel's criminal law as a rough tribal system that later civilizations improved upon. The text does not support it. Deuteronomy 19 distinguishes the man who killed by accident from the man who lay in wait, provides six cities of asylum spaced so that any Israelite could reach one, requires that the case be heard by the congregation, and forbids conviction on one witness. That is intent, asylum, due process and evidentiary standard, set down in an age when a blood feud was the ordinary remedy everywhere else.

The gospel figure in the arrangement is exact and is the reason the passage is more than jurisprudence. The manslayer's freedom depended entirely on a death he had nothing to do with — he waited in the city until the high priest died, and then went home. His guilt was real; his release was another man's. But the same law that gave the refuge closed it against the murderer, and would not let him hold the horns of the altar to save himself. Mercy in Scripture is never a way around justice; it is justice satisfied elsewhere, and the man who will not have the refuge on God's terms is taken from the altar.
roots_summary: Hebrew nakah nephesh (H5221 / H5315), to smite at the life; ratsach (H7523), to murder; miqlat (H4733), a refuge.
roots_lines: Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite, to strike; joined to nephesh it gives smite him mortally.
Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul, life; the blow is aimed at the life itself.
Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to murder; the verb of the sixth commandment, distinct from lawful killing.
Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a place of refuge; the six cities appointed for the manslayer.
Hebrew goel haddam (H1350 / H1818) — the avenger of blood; the kinsman with the right of pursuit.
usage: “smite him mortally that he die” — the blow aimed at the life.
“which killeth any person at unawares” — who the refuge was for.
“thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die” — no sanctuary for murder.

pos: v.i. (to suffer pain, especially as consequence; of the man who goes surety for a stranger)
etymology: From Old English smeortan, to be painful. At Proverbs 11:15 it renders Hebrew ra'a, to be broken or brought to evil — the older English sense of smart as a stinging pain rather than cleverness.
biblical_def:
Solomon returns to the subject of standing surety more often than to almost any other piece of financial counsel, and always the same way: He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure. The English holds a pun the Hebrew does not, and it is a useful one — to smart is to sting, and the man who guarantees a stranger's debt will feel it. Proverbs 6 opens with the same warning and treats it as an emergency: if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, go, humble thyself, and make sure thy friend... deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter. Get out tonight; do not give sleep to thine eyes.

The word is worth the entry for the older sense of smart, which has almost vanished from English. It means to feel a sharp consequence, and Scripture uses consequence as an ordinary instrument of instruction without apology. Proverbs is largely a book of them: the sluggard and his poverty, the drunkard and his woes, the adulterer and his wounds and dishonour. None of this is fatalism, and none of it denies grace. It is the created order's ordinary way of teaching, and a father who removes every consequence from a son's path is not being kind to him. What Proverbs will not do is let the sting be the last word. The book that says the surety shall smart for it is the same book that says a friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to feel a lively pungent pain; to feel the punishment or evil consequence of anything.
webster_full: SMART, v.i. To feel a lively pungent pain; to feel a pungent pain of mind; to feel the punishment of error or wrong.
SMART, n. Quick pungent lively pain; a pricking local pain, as the pain from puncture by nettles.
SURETISHIP, n. The state of being surety; the obligation of a person to answer for another.
SURETY, n. Security against loss or damage; one that is bound with and for another.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not of the family.
scriptures: Proverbs 11:15
He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure.
Proverbs 6:1
My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger,
Proverbs 22:26
Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts.
Hebrews 7:22
By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament.
corruption_summary: Consequence is treated as cruelty, and a generation shielded from every sting arrives at adulthood without the instruction Proverbs assumes a father will let life give.
corruption_paragraphs: A wide instinct now holds that a loving parent, church or society removes the sting from error. Proverbs assumes the opposite as a matter of course: the surety smarts, the sluggard goes hungry, the scorner finds no one to teach him. This is not harshness but the way a wise God built the world to instruct creatures who do not learn well from advice. The Reformed doctrine of the law's first use says the same thing in another register — the law restrains and exposes before it ever guides, and a man who has never felt its edge will not look for a Saviour.

The remarkable thing is where the Bible takes the word. Proverbs spends three warnings telling a man never to become surety for a stranger, because he will smart for it; and Hebrews says that Jesus was made a surety of a better testament. He did the one thing Solomon said no wise man should do. He struck hands for strangers — for those who were strangers from the covenants of promise — and He smarted for it to the last farthing. Proverbs describes the cost so that the reader will know what it meant when Christ paid it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'a (H7489), to be broken, to suffer harm; arab (H6148), to go surety; taqa kaph (H8628 / H3709), to strike the hand.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'a (H7489) — to be broken, to come to evil; the AV's shall smart for it.
Hebrew arab (H6148) — to pledge, to go surety; the same verb as Hezekiah's undertake for me.
Hebrew taqa kaph (H8628, H3709) — to strike the hand; the gesture that sealed a guarantee.
Hebrew zar (H2114) — a stranger, an outsider; the party Proverbs warns against guaranteeing.
Greek egguos (G1450) — a surety; the title given to the Lord Jesus in Hebrews 7:22.
usage: “He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it” — the sting named in advance.
“deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter” — Proverbs treating it as an emergency.
“Jesus made a surety of a better testament” — the one who did it anyway.

pos: n. pl. (those who stumble in speech; in Isaiah 32, they shall be ready to speak plainly)
etymology: From Old English stamerian, to stammer. At Isaiah 32:4 it renders Hebrew illeg, stuttering or stammering — used once in Scripture, in a promise about the coming reign of a King in righteousness.
biblical_def:
Isaiah 32 opens with a King who shall reign in righteousness, and the chapter describes His reign by what it repairs: And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken. The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly. Four disabilities, and each is both physical and spiritual in the prophets' usage — dim eyes, deaf ears, a rash heart, a stumbling tongue. Under the King they are mended, and the last promise is given to men who could not get their words out: they shall speak plainly.

The Bible is unusually attentive to impediments of speech. Moses objected to his commission on exactly this ground — I am not eloquent... I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue — and was not excused but answered: Who hath made man's mouth? Isaiah elsewhere turns the image into judgment, saying that since the people would not hear plain Hebrew, with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people — the incomprehensible speech of an invading army. And Paul, who was accused at Corinth of being contemptible in speech, made the accusation into the argument: he came not with excellency of speech, so that their faith should not stand in the wisdom of men. The gospel has never depended on fluency, and Isaiah 32 promises that the men whose tongues fail them now will one day speak plainly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who stammer; persons who hesitate or stumble in speaking.
webster_full: STAMMERER, n. One that stammers or hesitates in speaking.
STAMMER, v.i. To stop in uttering syllables or words; to hesitate or falter in speaking.
ELOQUENT, a. Having the power of oratory; speaking with fluency, propriety, elegance and animation.
PLAINLY, adv. In a plain manner; clearly; evidently; without disguise or ambiguity.
RASH, a. Hasty in counsel or action; precipitate; resolving or entering on a project without due deliberation.
scriptures: Isaiah 32:4
The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly.
Isaiah 32:3
And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken.
Exodus 4:10
And Moses said unto the LORD, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.
Isaiah 28:11
For with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people.
corruption_summary: Ministry is filtered by presentation, and the plain fact that God chose a man slow of speech to confront Pharaoh is preached but not practised.
corruption_paragraphs: The evangelical pulpit has been steadily conformed to the standards of the stage, and the men who rise in it are those who present well. Scripture's record runs strikingly the other way. Moses stammered and was sent anyway; Jeremiah said he could not speak, for he was a child; Paul was reckoned at Corinth to be weighty in his letters but weak in bodily presence and contemptible in speech, and answered by pointing out that the treasure is in earthen vessels that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. A church that screens for fluency is screening on a criterion the Holy Ghost does not appear to use.

The promise of Isaiah 32 also deserves to be heard by those who carry a real impediment. The chapter is about a King reigning in righteousness, and one of the marks of His reign is that the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly. That is not a demand made of them; it is something done for them. Until that day, the answer God gave Moses stands as the answer to every man who pleads his mouth as a reason to decline what he has been given: Who hath made man's mouth?... now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.
roots_summary: Hebrew illeg (H5926), stammering; laeg (H3934), of a foreign or mocking tongue; kebad peh (H3515 / H6310), heavy of mouth.
roots_lines: Hebrew illeg (H5926) — stammering; used once, in the promise of Isaiah 32:4.
Hebrew kebad peh (H3515, H6310) — heavy of mouth; Moses' description of himself at the bush.
Hebrew laeg (H3934) — stammering, foreign; the invading speech of Isaiah 28:11.
Hebrew tsachach (H6703) — clear, dazzling white; the root behind speak plainly.
Greek mogilalos (G3424) — having an impediment in speech; the man our Lord healed in Mark 7:32.
usage: “the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly” — a promise, not a demand.
“I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” — the objection God overruled.
“with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak” — the same image turned to judgment.

pos: adj. (unsteady, about to fall; David's figure for the men conspiring against him)
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Old English tealtrian, to be unsteady. At Psalm 62:3 it renders a Hebrew participle from dachah, to be thrust down — a fence already pushed and leaning.
biblical_def:
Psalm 62 is David under organized attack, and the psalm's power is in what it says about the attackers: How long will ye imagine mischief against a man? ye shall be slain all of you: as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence. He does not call them strong. A bowing wall and a tottering fence are structures that have already lost their integrity and are only waiting for the day they come down. The men plotting his ruin look formidable and are, in the psalm's judgment, leaning.

That verdict is possible only because of where David is standing, and the psalm says so twice in almost identical words: He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved. Rock against fence. The contrast runs through the whole psalm and comes to a head in the weighing-scale image a few verses later: men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity. Both ends of society, weighed, come up lighter than nothing. And the psalm ends with the ground of the confidence, a sentence the Reformers loved: power belongeth unto God, and, in the same breath, also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy. Power and mercy in one Person is why a man can call an army a tottering fence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): shaking as if about to fall; vacillating; standing unsteadily.
webster_full: TOTTERING, ppr. Shaking as if about to fall; vacillating; failing.
TOTTER, v.i. To shake so as to threaten a fall; to vacillate; to stand unsteadily.
FENCE, n. A wall, hedge, ditch, bank, or line of posts and rails, intended to confine beasts or to guard.
DEFENCE, n. That which opposes attack; protection; guard; also, a fortification.
BALANCE, n. A pair of scales; the instrument by which bodies are weighed.
scriptures: Psalm 62:3
How long will ye imagine mischief against a man? ye shall be slain all of you: as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence.
Psalm 62:2
He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
Psalm 62:5
My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.
Isaiah 40:30
Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall:
corruption_summary: Strength is assessed by present appearance, and a believer measuring an opposition by what it looks like today will always overrate it.
corruption_paragraphs: David's estimate of his enemies would have looked absurd to an observer. They were numerous, organized, and delighted in lies; he was the one in danger. He calls them a bowing wall. The judgment is not bravado but a different measurement: weighed in the balance, men of low degree and men of high degree alike come up lighter than vanity, because the weight in the other pan is God. A Christian who assesses opposition by how solid it looks this morning will be permanently afraid, and a Christian who has learned to weigh will be calm without being foolish.

There is no significant postmodern redefinition of this word to rebut. The principle to recover is the discipline in the psalm's refrain, which David speaks not to God but to himself: My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him. The only is the hard word. Most of us wait upon God and also upon three or four contingencies we are quietly counting on, and the psalm strips them out. When the expectation is from Him alone, the wall may lean as long as it likes.
roots_summary: Hebrew dachah (H1760), to thrust down; gader (H1447), a fence or wall; tsur (H6697), a rock.
roots_lines: Hebrew dachah (H1760) — to thrust or push down; the participle rendered tottering.
Hebrew gader (H1447) — a fence, a hedge of stones; what the conspirators are compared to.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — a rock, a cliff; what God is to the man they are conspiring against.
Hebrew misgab (H4869) — a high tower, a defence; the second figure in the refrain.
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, vanity; what both high and low weigh in the balance.
usage: “as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence” — an army weighed and found leaning.
“He only is my rock and my salvation” — the other pan of the scale.
“My soul, wait thou only upon God” — the hard word is only.
